abstract: Altered protein glycosylation accompanies many diseases and can influence drug binding, yet the contributions of specific glycan features remain difficult to resolve within heterogeneous glycoprotein populations. Here, we combined sequential enzymatic glycan remodeling, composition-resolved variable-temperature native mass spectrometry (vT-nMS), complementary glycosylation analyses, and molecular modelling to investigate warfarin binding to the F1 and S variants of human 1-acid glycoprotein (AGP). Measured affinities spanned more than an order of magnitude across the glycan compositions and remodeled samples examined. Core 1-6 fucosylation favored binding by both variants and shifted the thermodynamics toward less favorable enthalpy and more favorable entropy. Antennary fucosylation generally weakened binding in F1 and had more variable effects in S. Weaker binding was associated with a less favorable entropic contribution despite more favorable enthalpy. Outer-arm trimming produced variant-dependent effects, including changes in enthalpic and entropic contributions that were partly obscured by comparatively small changes in affinity. Endo F3-mediated truncation also produced distinct responses in the two variants. Within the F1 truncation series, the three-core population exhibited the strongest binding and greatest enthalpic stabilization, whereas the corresponding S population exhibited a more favorable entropic contribution than F1 without a comparable affinity enhancement. No warfarin complexes were detected for compositions assigned as containing bisecting GlcNAc. Molecular simulations and reconstructed glycan ensembles suggested that changes in glycan orientation and glycan-protein interactions near the binding-funnel entrance may contribute to the observed binding effects. Together, these findings reveal how glycan structure and protein sequence jointly determine the affinity and thermodynamic balance of ligand recognition and demonstrate the value of composition-resolved vT-nMS for dissecting functional heterogeneity in glycoprotein populations.
